# Dvayatānupassanā Sutta (Snp 3.12 (PTS Snp 139))

**ID:** Snp 3.12 (PTS Snp 139)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dvayatānupassanā Sutta* ("Contemplating Pairs", Snp 3.12) is the twelfth discourse of the Mahāvagga, the third chapter of the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1983; SuttaCentral]. Characterized by Bhikkhu Sujato as the longest and most doctrinally substantial discourse in the *Suttanipāta*, it outlines a meditative method of contemplation (*anupassanā*) organized around a sequence of dualities or pairs (*dvayatā*), in which suffering (*dukkha*) consistently constitutes the second term [Norman 1983; Sujato 2012]. The discourse demonstrates how each pair is causally connected, showing that contemplating the origination and cessation of suffering leads directly toward liberation; an ardent and resolute practitioner can expect either full awakening in this life or the state of non-return [Norman 1983; Sujato 2012; SuttaCentral].

Doctrinally, the text expounds conditionality across multiple causal series, highlighting how suffering arises in dependence on factors such as preparations (*saṅkhāras*), sustenance (*āhāra*), initiative (*ārambha*), and perturbation (*iñjita*) [Dayal 1932; Anālayo 2010]. With the cessation and calming of *saṅkhāras*, no further suffering arises and future rebirth is averted [Anālayo 2010]. Scholars such as Har Dayal, Louis de la Vallée Poussin, and K. R. Norman have examined the sutta's relation to early Buddhist dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), discussing whether the standard twelvefold formula was developed by recasting these primitive pairs—described by some as a "primitive fragment of Abhidhamma"—alongside discourses such as the *Kalahavivāda Sutta* [Dayal 1932; Norman 1983]. Katukurunde Ñāṇananda also emphasizes the sutta's analysis of sense restraint and conceptualization (*maññanā*), quoting its declaration that whatever people conceptualize turns out otherwise, exposing the deceptiveness of sensory reality [Ñāṇananda 1971].

SuttaCentral records extensive passage-level parallels across canonical collections, including the *Santatara Sutta* (Iti 73), *Cālā Sutta* (SN 5.6), *Upasena Sutta* (Ud 4.9), *Taṇhuppāda Sutta* (AN 4.9; Iti 105), *Paṭhamarūpārāmasutta* (SN 35.136), Jātaka 493, Sanskrit and Tibetan versions of the *Udānavarga* (UV 32, UVS 32, Uv Kg 32, T 212, T 213), and Chinese Āgama parallels (SF 199, T 765), while noting its citation in the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 1) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates these links through dense Pali-internal reuse with AN 4, SN 35, SN 56, and the commentaries, while cross-language algorithmic alignments connect the sutta to the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) and *Ekottarikāgama* (T 125), Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* texts, the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, and the Tibetan *Catuḥsatya-sūtra* [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral].
